title: Stage 9 — Authentication & Authorization
goal: Add secure user accounts to the API — register, login, JWT access tokens, refresh tokens, and role-based access.
summary: Backend-first auth: prove every endpoint in Postman before building login screens in the next stage.

checkpoint.prompt: "Only the owner can delete this workout" is an example of…
checkpoint.explanation: Authentication = identity. Authorization = permissions after identity is known.

checkpoint.prompt: How should passwords be stored in the database?

choices.text: Hashed with a slow algorithm (bcrypt, argon2) — never plain text
Plain text for easy password resets

checkpoint.explanation: Hashing is one-way. If the DB leaks, attackers still can't read passwords.

checkpoint.prompt: How does the client send a JWT access token on protected requests?
checkpoint.explanation: Bearer tokens go in the Authorization header. The server verifies the signature before trusting claims.

checkpoint.prompt: Access tokens expire in 15 minutes. Why also issue a refresh token?

choices.text: Get a new access token without asking for the password again
Browsers require two tokens by law

checkpoint.explanation: Short-lived access tokens limit damage if stolen. Refresh tokens renew access with a longer-lived, revocable credential.

checkpoint.prompt: A logged-in user with role `user` hits DELETE /admin/users. Server returns 403. Why?

choices.text: Authenticated but not authorized — admin role required
DELETE is never allowed over HTTP

checkpoint.explanation: 401 = not logged in. 403 = logged in but lacking permission. RBAC checks role after auth middleware.

checklist.label: Users table with hashed passwords and role column
POST /auth/refresh issues a new access token
GET /me returns current user when Bearer token is valid
Protected routes return 401 without token; admin routes return 403 for non-admin
Postman collection proves register → login → me → refresh flow

questions.prompt: Login with email and password proves…
questions.explanation: Login verifies identity. Authorization rules apply after the server knows who you are.

questions.prompt: Why hash passwords with bcrypt instead of storing them plain text?

choices.text: One-way hashing protects users if the database leaks
Plain text is faster to compare at login
bcrypt encrypts passwords so you can decrypt them later

questions.explanation: Hashing is one-way. bcrypt.compare checks a guess without ever storing the original password.

questions.prompt: A JWT access token typically contains…

choices.text: Signed claims like user id and role — not the password
The user's plain-text password for convenience

questions.explanation: JWTs carry claims the server signed. Never put secrets or passwords inside a token.

questions.prompt: GET /me with no Authorization header should return…
questions.explanation: No token means the server doesn't know who you are — that's 401, not 403.

questions.prompt: Why keep access tokens short-lived and use refresh tokens?

choices.text: Limits damage from a stolen access token; refresh can be revoked server-side
JWTs cannot expire without a refresh token
Refresh tokens are sent on every API request instead of access tokens

questions.explanation: Short access + long refresh is the standard tradeoff: security vs user convenience.
